paper_summary: This paper introduces GRADINO, a from-scratch benchmark generator for automatically verifiable numerical question answering over multiple non-relational tables. GRADINO synthesizes a latent relational source (schema and table contents), derives executable SQL programs to compute gold answers, and then renders answer-preserving perturbed non-relational views (pivoted/hierarchical headers, merged columns, blank rows/columns, typographical noise, N/A values, unit heterogeneity and conversions, OCR-like errors). It supports two multi-table evidence-flow patterns: parallel (extract a scalar from each table, then aggregate via SUM/AVG/MAX/MIN) and sequential (propagate lookup keys across a chain of tables, then aggregate). The system verbalizes SQL into NL questions and verifies/verifies+repairs them automatically. The authors use GRADINO to evaluate multiple LLMs (gpt-5-mini and Qwen-family models) across environmental and financial domains, quantify sharp performance drops with increasing table count and with unit heterogeneity, validate generated-question correctness manually (~95.9% correct), and show GRADINO-generated data can supplement scarce in-domain training data to improve downstream performance. Code and generated datasets are released.
summary_of_strengths: 1) Novel, well-motivated generator: GRADINO fills an important gap in Table QA evaluation by enabling controlled, verifiable generation of multi-table numerical QA over non-relational table views. 2) Methodological design: separation of a latent relational source (for SQL supervision and verifiability) from rendered non-relational views is conceptually clean and enables systematic perturbation and control of reasoning topology, table count, and unit conventions. 3) Empirical findings: clear, reproducible evidence that non-relational formatting, unit heterogeneity, and multi-table scaling cause large, compounded accuracy drops in current LLMs; sequential vs. parallel regimes are analyzed separately. 4) Practical utility: GRADINO data can be used to fine-tune models and complements scarce in-domain multi-table benchmarks. 5) Release: code, prompts, and generated datasets are provided, improving community value and reproducibility.
summary_of_weaknesses: 1) Synthetic realism: GRADINO generates data from scratch; while this enables control, it may not capture all distributional, visual, and semantic idiosyncrasies of real spreadsheets/reports (authors acknowledge this). External validity to all real-world documents may therefore be limited. 2) Generator-model dependence and potential bias: GRADINO uses an LLM internally (gpt-5-mini) for schema and question generation and also evaluates gpt-5-mini; although the paper argues the main failure modes stem from rendering, there remains a risk of favorable bias or subtle contamination that could advantage that model. 3) Limited real-table validation: validation on perturbed real tables is valuable but uses a small set of tables (constrained by which relational tables can be plausibly pivoted), so transfer claims to real-world corpora would be stronger with broader validation. 4) Sequential realism constraint: the sequential regime enforces unique lookup matches for evaluation clarity; while understandable, this reduces realism (many real chains may introduce ambiguities or multiple matches). 5) Question-generation errors concentrated in sequential cases: the manual check shows lower fidelity for sequential verbalization; fixing this may require stronger backbone LLMs or additional constraints.
comments_suggestions_typos: Minor suggestions: (a) expand real-table validation if possible (more domains / documents) and report failure examples from real tables; (b) more ablations to quantify generator-model favoritism (e.g., generate with one model family and test with disjoint families); (c) consider extending renderings to include visual alignment cues and chart-table mixtures or at least discuss more concretely how those could be incorporated; (d) release full prompts and a reproducibility checklist (they appear to release prompts in appendix—good) and report the fraction of generations discarded per regime (they report this but ensure clarity in main text); (e) small typos/flow issues: none major—paper is well organized.
limitations_and_societal_impact: The authors discuss many limitations (synthetic realism, restricted numerical structure, question-verbalization errors, discarded invalid generations) and ethical considerations (use of fictional data, use of public datasets for validation). Missing or under-emphasized items: (a) visual/layout cues and figure/table mixtures are noted but deserve more discussion with respect to models that use multimodal/layout features; (b) locale and language diversity for unit conventions and their impact on non-English datasets; (c) stronger explicit analysis of generator-model favoritism when proprietary LLMs are used for generation and verification; (d) implications for high-stakes domains (finance/environmental reporting) where small silent numerical errors have real consequences—practical mitigations or human-in-the-loop recommendations could be emphasized more.
ethical_concerns: No major ACL Code of Ethics violations identified. The paper uses synthetic fictional entities and public, research-use databases for validation. The authors disclose use of LLMs in generation and the limits of the benchmark. The only caution: reliance on proprietary LLMs for generation/verification could create reproducibility and bias concerns, but these are discussed and do not constitute an ethical violation.
